title: Unexpected breech birth
blurb: Recognise a breech in labour, support the woman's choice, keep hands off, know when and how to intervene, and get neonatal help ready (RCOG GTG 20b, NICE NG121).
question: Nadia is labouring at home with her second baby. As she pushes, the midwife sees buttocks, not a head, at the perineum. Birth is imminent. What is the midwife's best approach?

teach.body: A breech presentation is a baby lying bottom or feet first. It is 'unexpected' when it is first recognised in labour, sometimes only when the buttocks are seen. Formally, RCOG GTG 20b advises a 'hands off' approach to vaginal breech birth: no traction on the baby. In plain English: let the woman's pushing and gravity do the work, watch the clock, and step in with specific manoeuvres only when there is delay or the baby's condition is poor.

Discuss the benefits and risks of vaginal birth and caesarean: caesarean raises the chance of serious problems for the woman; vaginal breech birth raises the chance of serious problems for the baby. Explain that any benefit of caesarean for the baby may be greater in early labour. Offer a choice between continuing labour and caesarean. Near or in the active second stage, caesarean is not routinely offered (GTG 20b).

teach.h: The sequence of a vaginal breech birth

steps.label: Arms
steps.sub: Usually born spontaneously; if not, elbow flexion or Lovset's

items: The midwife sees buttocks advancing with each push; birth is imminent, so transfer before the birth is not safe.
She asks Nadia's partner to call 999, calls for the second midwife, and gets the resuscitation equipment ready and warm.
She explains calmly to Nadia what is happening and encourages her to push with contractions, keeping her hands off.
She notes the time the buttocks and the umbilicus are born. The arms and head deliver within 3 minutes.
The baby is dried and assessed for newborn life support; the hips will need a NIPE hip ultrasound as she was breech at birth.

teach.text: Traction is the classic error. Pulling on the baby can extend the arms and head, which makes the birth harder and risks head entrapment. 'Hands off' plus the clock is the safe approach; manoeuvres are for delay or a poor condition, not routine.

items: In labour, discuss risks and benefits and offer a choice between continuing labour and caesarean (NG121).
Near or in the active second stage, caesarean is not routinely offered (GTG 20b).
Hands off: no traction. Intervene if more than 5 minutes buttocks-to-head or 3 minutes umbilicus-to-head, or the baby is in poor condition.
Hold the bony pelvic girdle; arms by elbow flexion or Lovset's; head by Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit or forceps.
Call for help and neonatal support; breech at birth is a NIPE hip risk factor.

summary: You can now support a woman who presents in labour with a breech baby, explain her options, and manage a hands-off vaginal breech birth with the correct time limits. You can also name the manoeuvres for delay, avoid traction and the Burns-Marshall method, and arrange neonatal care and hip screening.

A.q: During an unexpected vaginal breech birth, the baby's buttocks and legs have been born. What is the recommended approach while birth continues?
options: Gentle traction on the legs with contractions
Fundal pressure to speed the birth
Rotating the baby to face upwards
A.why: RCOG GTG 20b advises a hands-off approach with no traction on the baby; intervention is reserved for delay or poor fetal condition.

whyNot.0: Traction is specifically advised against: it can cause extension of the arms and head.
whyNot.2: Fundal pressure is not part of the GTG 20b hands-off approach.
whyNot.3: Routine rotation is an intervention; GTG 20b advises letting the birth progress without handling.

A.q: During a breech birth, how long after the birth of the umbilicus should the midwife intervene if the head has not been born?
A.why: GTG 20b: intervene if more than 3 minutes pass from the birth of the umbilicus to the head (or more than 5 minutes from the buttocks).

whyNot.0: 1 minute is shorter than the GTG 20b trigger for umbilicus-to-head delay.
whyNot.2: 5 minutes is the buttocks-to-head limit, not umbilicus-to-head.
whyNot.3: 10 minutes far exceeds both GTG 20b time limits.

A.q: If the midwife needs to hold the baby's body during a breech birth, where should the baby be held?
A.why: GTG 20b: if handling is needed, grasp the baby by the bony pelvic girdle, not the soft tissues of the abdomen.

whyNot.0: Holding the abdomen risks injury to the baby's internal organs.
whyNot.1: Holding by the ankles encourages traction and gives poor control.
whyNot.3: The armpits are not accessible until the arms are born and are not the recommended hold.

B.q: During a breech birth the baby's arms are extended above the head and the birth has stalled. Which manoeuvre is appropriate?
B.why: GTG 20b: extended arms can be delivered by elbow flexion or Lovset's manoeuvre.

whyNot.0: McRoberts is a manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia in a cephalic birth.
whyNot.1: Burns-Marshall is a method for the after-coming head and is not advised.
whyNot.2: Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit is for delivering the after-coming head, not the arms.

B.q: During a breech birth the after-coming head is delayed. Which manoeuvre does RCOG GTG 20b support?
B.why: GTG 20b: the after-coming head can be delivered by Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit or forceps; Burns-Marshall is not advised.

whyNot.1: GTG 20b advises against the Burns-Marshall method.
whyNot.2: Suprapubic pressure is used for an impacted anterior shoulder in shoulder dystocia.
whyNot.3: Lovset's manoeuvre delivers extended arms, not the head.

B.q: A woman in early labour is found to have a breech baby on admission. What does NICE NG121 advise the midwife and obstetrician to do?
options: Offer a choice of labour or caesarean
B.why: NG121 1.15.3: offer women in labour with breech presentation a choice between continuing labour and caesarean, after discussing the benefits and risks.

whyNot.0: Caesarean is one option, but it should be offered as a choice after discussion, not imposed.
whyNot.1: ECV is an antenatal option from 36 weeks for women not in labour.
whyNot.3: NICE requires a discussion of benefits and risks so she can make an informed choice.

C.q: At a home birth, Esther is actively pushing and the midwife sees the baby's buttocks distending the perineum. Birth is imminent. What is the best action?
options: Transfer her by car to hospital
Ask her to stop pushing until help arrives
Apply traction to speed the birth
Call 999 and prepare for a hands-off birth
C.why: With birth imminent, transfer is unsafe. Call for help (999 and the second midwife), prepare neonatal resuscitation equipment, and support a hands-off breech birth (GTG 20b).

whyNot.0: Transfer during an imminent breech birth risks the baby being born in transit without support.
whyNot.1: Asking her to stop pushing does not stop the birth and can cause dangerous delay.
whyNot.2: Traction is advised against; it risks extension of the arms and head.

C.q: During a breech birth the umbilicus was born 4 minutes ago. The baby's body is pale and floppy and the head has not been born. What should the midwife do?
options: Pull firmly on the baby's trunk
Ask her to change to all fours
C.why: More than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head, together with poor fetal condition, are GTG 20b triggers to intervene with manoeuvres.

whyNot.0: Waiting longer increases the risk of hypoxic injury once the time limit and poor condition are present.
whyNot.2: Traction is advised against and risks extension of the head and entrapment.
whyNot.3: A position change alone does not deal with a delayed after-coming head in a compromised baby.

C.q: A baby girl was born by unexpected vaginal breech birth at 39 weeks and is well. Which follow-up is specifically indicated by the NIPE programme?
C.why: Breech presentation at or after 36 weeks (or at birth from 28 weeks) is a NIPE hip risk factor, so a hip ultrasound is arranged.

whyNot.1: A cranial ultrasound is not a NIPE screening requirement after breech birth.
whyNot.2: An echocardiogram is not indicated by breech presentation.
whyNot.3: Breech birth is not an indication for repeat hearing screening.

reteach.title: Think 'watch, wait, time, then act'
reteach.question: If a breech baby will usually be born by the woman's own efforts, what exactly is the midwife there to do?

blocks.body: Her job is to watch, encourage, keep the time and be ready. Most breech babies are born with no handling. Touching or pulling tends to make the baby's arms and chin lift, which is what causes trouble. So hands stay off while things progress. The clock (5 minutes from buttocks, 3 minutes from umbilicus) and the baby's tone and colour tell her when to act.

blocks.text: Lovset's is for the ARMS; Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit is for the HEAD. Burns-Marshall is not advised.

explain.body: Discuss benefits and risks of vaginal birth and caesarean; any benefit of caesarean for the baby may be greater in early labour; offer a choice (NG121 1.15.1-1.15.3). Near or in active second stage, caesarean is not routinely offered (GTG 20b).

test.q: A woman in early labour has a breech baby and asks about caesarean. What should she be told about timing?
options: Any benefit for the baby may be greater now
Caesarean is safer once fully dilated
Timing makes no difference to the baby
Caesarean is best after waters break
test.why: NG121 1.15.2: any benefit of caesarean in reducing serious problems for the baby may be greater in early labour.

whyNot.1: Near or in the active second stage, caesarean is not routinely offered (GTG 20b).
whyNot.2: NICE states that the benefit for the baby may be greater in early labour, so timing matters.
whyNot.3: There is no NICE advice to wait for membrane rupture.

explain.body: No traction. Let maternal effort deliver the baby. If handling is needed, hold the bony pelvic girdle, never the soft abdomen (GTG 20b).

steps.label: Act on delay or poor condition

test.q: Why is traction on the baby advised against during a vaginal breech birth?
options: It slows the second stage of labour
It can extend the arms and head
It increases the risk of cord prolapse
test.why: Traction encourages extension of the arms and head, making the birth harder and risking head entrapment.

whyNot.0: The concern is not slowing labour but causing extension of the arms and head.
whyNot.2: Cord prolapse risk relates to membrane rupture with a poorly applied presenting part, not traction at birth.
whyNot.3: Perineal trauma is not the reason GTG 20b gives for avoiding traction.

explain.body: Intervene if more than 5 minutes from buttocks to head, more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head, or poor fetal condition. Arms: elbow flexion or Lovset's. Head: Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit or forceps (GTG 20b).

test.q: The buttocks of a breech baby were born 6 minutes ago and the head is not yet born. What does this indicate?
options: Normal progress for a breech birth
test.why: More than 5 minutes from the birth of the buttocks to the head is a GTG 20b trigger to intervene with manoeuvres.

whyNot.0: 6 minutes exceeds the 5-minute limit, so this is not normal progress.
whyNot.1: Oxytocin at this stage would not resolve a delayed after-coming head.
whyNot.2: With the body born, manoeuvres to deliver the head are needed, not caesarean.

explain.body: Call for help early: a second midwife or 999 at home, and the obstetric and neonatal teams in hospital. Prepare warm towels and resuscitation equipment. After birth, breech presentation is a NIPE hip risk factor for ultrasound.

test.q: In hospital, a midwife recognises a breech presentation in a woman who is fully dilated and pushing. Who should she call?
test.why: A breech birth may need obstetric manoeuvres and neonatal resuscitation, so both teams should attend.

whyNot.1: Near or in the active second stage caesarean is not routinely offered, so the priority is obstetric and neonatal support at the birth.
whyNot.2: The manager can help with staffing, but the baby and woman need obstetric and neonatal clinicians.
whyNot.3: Physiotherapy has no role in an imminent breech birth.
